extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geographers, meteorologists, and scientifically literate readers of physical geography/meteorology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical standards for observing and interpreting climatic, hygrometric, electric, and altitudinal phenomena in physical geography and plant distribution. Emphasizes measurement practice, comparative tables, and the multiple factors controlling vegetation and snow-lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermic scale of cultivation / plant thermal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange plants on a thermic scale beginning with those requiring the hottest climates (e.g., vanilla, cacao, banana, cocoa-nut) and proceeding through pineapple, sugar-cane, coffee, date-trees, cotton, citrons, olives, edible chestnuts, and vines producing potable wine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this ordering to compare limits of cultivation on plains and mountain slopes; note that this scale implies more than mean annual temperature — other climatic relations (seasonality, light, humidity) are involved. References: Humboldt, Meyen, Boussingault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viticulture temperature thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: For producing 'potable' wine it is requisite that the mean annual heat should exceed 49 degrees, with a specified higher winter/some-season temperature (text gives 'winter temperature upward of 64 degrees').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical thresholds illustrated by table of European stations (Bordeaux, Berlin, Wurzburg, etc.). Use these thresholds as practical benchmarks but interpret alongside seasonality and insolation; comparisons caution that similar shaded-thermometer readings can give different ripening outcomes where light differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to measure insolation (photometry) separately from thermometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of solar influence cannot be inferred from shade-thermometer readings alone; a Photometer (measuring light) must be used to understand why thermometric similarities may yield different biological results (e.g., vine ripeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on thermometers suspended in the shade; include photometric measurements to quantify light intensity and its biological effect. Anti-pattern: concluding sunlight effects from shaded-thermometer data without photometric evidence ('Nullo adhibito Photometro, haud cognosces').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of thermometers in shade for surface temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: A thermometer standing in the shade and protected from direct insolation and nocturnal radiation cannot always indicate the true superficial temperature of the ground exposed to the sun's rays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing temperature effects on vegetation or surface processes, account for the discrepancy between shaded-air thermometer readings and actual ground-surface temperatures influenced by direct solar heating and nocturnal radiation. Use complementary measurements or inferences (e.g., Dove's Chiswick Gardens data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple climatic relations beyond mean annual temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits of cultivation depend not only on mean annual temperature but also on other climatic relations: seasonal temperatures, late frosts, spring/summer/autumn means, light intensity, moisture/precipitation patterns, and wind regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing agricultural or biogeographic limits, evaluate seasonal means (winter, spring, summer, autumn), frequency of damaging events (e.g., late May frosts), and insolation differences (cloudy vs bright skies). Use tables of seasonal averages and long-term observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triadic relation for isothermal systems (vertical vs latitudinal correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In each isothermal system there is a close and necessary connection between: (1) the decrease of heat with vertical elevation (lapse rate), (2) the difference of temperature per degree of latitude, and (3) the equivalence between the mean temperature of a mountain station and that at a sea-level point of different latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-element relation when comparing climates of mountain stations to sea-level latitudes. Example: Central Europe lapse/latitude correspondences permit equating high-elevation temperatures to much higher-latitude sea-level climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional lapse-rate quantification and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate of temperature decrease with elevation (lapse rate) must be quantified regionally: e.g., Central Europe ~1.8 degrees per 534 feet (~1 degree per 267 ft); parts of the tropical Cordilleras ~1 degree per 341 feet (Boussingault ~319 ft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a universal lapse rate; determine or adopt region-specific values based on observations. Use such lapse rates to convert elevation differences to approximate latitudinal temperature equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of snow-line phenomena and controlling causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the 'limit of perpetual snow' distinguish it from (a) annual fluctuation of the snow-line, (b) sporadic falls of snow, and (c) the existence of glaciers; the snow-line is controlled by multiple factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the following controlling causes: differences in seasonal temperatures; prevailing wind directions and their land/sea relations; dryness or humidity of upper air strata; total thickness of accumulated snow; relation of snow-line to total mountain height; position within the chain; steepness of slope; proximity to other perpetually snowy summits; elevation/type (sea-coast vs interior) and nature (wooded vs grass vs rocky/wet) of surrounding plains. Use extensive determinations across latitudes and elevations (see Humboldt's tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of extensive comparative measurements across latitudes and altitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate understanding of temperature distribution, snow-line, and related phenomena requires numerous determinations across a wide range of latitudes and elevations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile comparative tables (isothermal lines, snow-line heights, seasonal means) and use multi-year observations to establish regularities and detect local exceptions. Footnoted references and published tables are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hygrometric measurement standard (psychrometry / dew point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use August's psychrometer, framed according to Dalton and Daniell, to determine the relative quantity of vapor (hygrometric condition) by means of the difference between dew point and air temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ psychrometers for quantitative humidity work; report dew point and temperature together. Cite example readings (e.g., Boussingault, Gay-Lussac, and Chiswick aerostatic ascent values) and be cautious about instrument and site comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize precipitation form/frequency over absolute vapor for biological effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of atmospheric moisture on organisms is not so much a consequence of absolute vapor content as of the nature and frequency of precipitation (dew, mist, rain, snow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ecological or agricultural impacts, document types and frequency of precipitation and local microclimatic phenomena (e.g., frequent mists of Paramos), not merely integrated vapor amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful hygrometric comparison between elevations (avoid assumptions of drier mountain air)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent observers have raised doubts about the asserted greater dryness of mountain air based on earlier hygrometric measurements; elevation comparisons require careful instrumentation and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-examine earlier claims (Saussure, Humboldt) in light of newer work (Kämtz, Bravais, Martins); ensure instrument calibration and comparable measurement protocols when comparing humidity across elevations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for atmospheric electricity observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Electrometric observations indicate an increase of general positive electricity with altitude and with the absence of trees, plus daily and seasonal variations and differences between continental and oceanic regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use electrometers (e.g., Colladon's electro-magnetic apparatus) and document altitude, surface cover (land/sea/vegetation), and timing (daily/seasonal). Note phenomena such as rapid transitions of sign (positive to negative) before/during fogs, snow, and storms; cite controlled experimental setups (limitations noted by Humboldt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider surface type (sea vs land, islands) in electric/storm dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric equilibrium is less frequently disturbed where the aerial ocean rests on a liquid base than over land; small insular groups can affect atmospheric condition and occasion storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In studies of storm formation and atmospheric electricity include underlying surface type as a factor; document local island effects and contrasts between maritime and continental environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud electrification and color-to-polarity association (empirical observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation into clouds increases electric tension of the external surface proportionally; experiments (Peltier) associate slate-gray clouds with negative electricity and white/red/orange clouds with positive electricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record cloud color and electrometric sign but also note conflicting findings among investigators (Lame, Becquerel, Peltier). Treat color-charge correlations as empirical and contested, not definitive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of lightning forms and durations (Arago)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arago's investigations distinguish three kinds of lightning: (1) zigzag, sharply defined at the edges; (2) sheets of light illuminating whole clouds; (3) globular lightning (fire-balls) — the first two last scarcely the thousandth part of a second, while globular lightning may remain visible for several seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting electrical discharges, classify observed lightning by form and measure/estimate duration. Use forms to relate to cloud structure and electromagnetic processes; cite Arago for methodology and typology.
